front: What is a Project template used for in a team setting?
back:
A **Project template** is a pre-configured Project — with instructions and optionally seed knowledge documents — that a team copies when spinning up a new work stream of the same type. Instead of rebuilding the instruction set from scratch for each new client engagement, product launch, or report cycle, the team starts from a known-good baseline.

Templates enforce consistency at the *creation* stage. They do not prevent drift after the copy is made; ongoing governance still requires review and update discipline for each live Project.
hook: Template = consistent starting point; it does not prevent drift after copying.

front: What does 'context persistence across sessions' mean in a Project?
back:
**Context persistence** means that instructions, knowledge documents, and conversation history stored inside a Project remain available in every future session opened within that Project — you do not start from a blank slate each time.

This is the defining advantage over a standard chat, where context is lost when the conversation ends. The practical impact is that you can pick up a multi-week piece of work and Claude still knows the constraints, tone requirements, and background information set up at the start — provided those are in the Project, not just mentioned once in an earlier chat.
hook: Project context survives session endings; single-chat context disappears when you close.

front: Why are duplicate documents in a knowledge base a problem?
back:
**Duplicate documents** — two copies of the same content, or near-identical versions — make it impossible to know which is the current, authoritative source. If one copy was updated and the other was not, Claude may draw on either and produce outputs that cite the wrong version.

Duplication often happens when a document is added under a slightly different filename without removing the original. The fix is to treat the knowledge base as a single-source repository: search before adding, and remove any predecessor document when uploading a new version.
hook: Duplicates make currency ambiguous — treat the knowledge base as a single-source repository.

front: What is the purpose of per-chat custom instructions (outside a Project)?
back:
**Per-chat custom instructions** (also called default instructions at the account level) are a standing personal preference set that applies to all conversations by default — preferred response length, language, tone, topics to avoid — without needing a full Project.

They differ from Project instructions in scope: per-chat instructions apply everywhere unless overridden by something more specific; Project instructions apply only inside that Project and can be more precise and contextual. A user who has no Project-specific setup but still wants consistent formatting across all Claude interactions uses per-chat instructions for that.
hook: Per-chat default instructions = personal preferences across all chats, no Project required.

front: Why does naming and organising Projects matter?
back:
When a team has many Projects, **clear names and descriptions** are the only navigational aid — there is no internal search across Project contents from the Project list. A name like "Q3 2025 Client ABC Proposal" is immediately legible; "New Project (3)" is not.

Organisation also matters for governance: when reviewing which Projects have access to sensitive knowledge documents, administrators need to identify each Project's purpose at a glance. Unintuitive naming creates audit blind spots.
hook: Clear Project names = navigable for users and auditable for administrators.

front: What does 'knowledge document freshness' mean?
back:
**Freshness** refers to how closely a knowledge document reflects the current state of the information it describes. A fresh document accurately represents today's policy, pricing, process, or product; a stale one reflects a past state that may no longer be true.

Freshness is not automatic — documents do not update themselves. It requires the knowledge base owner to schedule reviews and replace documents when the underlying reality changes. The risk of stale documents is that Claude produces confidently stated but outdated answers, and users may not detect the error without independent verification.
hook: Freshness = current and accurate; staleness produces confidently wrong answers.

front: What does configuring tone at the Project level accomplish?
back:
**Tone configuration** in Project instructions tells Claude the register to maintain across all conversations: formal or conversational, direct or diplomatic, technical or accessible. This ensures that every team member's output using the Project carries the same voice — important for client-facing work, brand-consistent communications, or regulated documents where a specific register is required.

Tone configuration does not eliminate the need for per-task specificity. An instruction that says "always write in formal English" will apply uniformly, but an individual conversation may still legitimately override it if the task demands a different register.
hook: Project-level tone = consistent voice for all users; individual chats can still override.

front: Per-chat file upload vs permanent Project knowledge — how do you decide which to use?
back:
Use **permanent knowledge** for material that is relevant to *many* conversations in the Project — brand guidelines, standing policies, product specs that every task references. The benefit is that users do not re-upload the same documents repeatedly.

Use a **per-chat upload** for material that is unique to *one* conversation — today's contract draft, a specific dataset being analysed, a client brief just received. Adding conversation-specific content to the permanent knowledge base pollutes it with ephemeral material that future conversations may incorrectly draw on.

The test: will more than one conversation need this document? If yes, knowledge base. If no, per-chat.
hook: Permanent knowledge = reused across sessions; per-chat = this conversation only.

front: What are three signs that project instructions have become unmaintainable?
back:
First, **internal contradictions** — rules that conflict with each other, indicating additions were made without reviewing the whole set. Second, **specificity rot** — instructions that name specific people, tools, or product versions that have since changed, making the instructions partly incorrect. Third, **length inflation** — a growing block of text that no one reads fully before adding another rule, meaning new rules may duplicate or contradict existing ones without anyone noticing.

Maintainable instructions are short, modular, and reviewed as a whole whenever a change is made — not merely appended to.
hook: Contradictions, outdated specifics, and unchecked length are the three maintainability failure modes.

front: What are signals that a Project knowledge base has started to accumulate scope creep?
back:
The clearest signals are: (1) **users cannot describe what the knowledge base contains** without opening it; (2) documents from previous projects or contexts are still present; (3) the base contains multiple versions of the same document; (4) topics represented span several unrelated domains, meaning no single task would benefit from more than a fraction of the content.

Scope creep degrades retrieval quality and makes auditing harder. The remedy is a periodic curation pass where every document is evaluated against a single question: "Will conversations in this Project regularly need this?"
hook: If nobody knows what the knowledge base contains, scope creep has already happened.

front: What is the risk of splitting a document that is genuinely unified?
back:
When a coherent argument or policy is split across multiple documents, Claude must retrieve and stitch together fragments to answer a question. If retrieval surfaces only some fragments, the answer is **incomplete or misleading** — Claude may state part of the rule without the qualifications or context that appears in the missing fragment.

Splitting is beneficial only when sections are independently useful. For a document where Section B's meaning depends on Section A's definitions, splitting produces two documents that are neither complete nor correctly usable in isolation. Splitting should follow topic boundaries, not page or length limits.
hook: Split only where sections are independently useful; splitting unified content breaks meaning.

front: How does a connector keep knowledge current, and what is the residual risk?
back:
A **connector** queries the linked external system at the time the conversation runs, so the content Claude receives reflects the current state of that system rather than a historical snapshot. Freshness is largely automatic as long as the source system is kept current.

The residual risk is **source dependency**: if the external system is unavailable, returns an error, or is itself out of date, Claude either cannot retrieve the content or returns stale data — and the user may not realise the source was unreachable. Connectors are not a substitute for keeping the source system governed and maintained.
hook: Connector currency depends on the source system being reachable and current — both must be true.

front: What steps should a team follow when handing off a shared Project to a new owner?
back:
The new owner should: (1) **read the full instruction set** to understand the existing rules and their purpose; (2) **audit the knowledge base** for stale, superseded, or out-of-scope documents; (3) **verify access permissions** to confirm only the right team members have edit rights; (4) **document the project purpose** in the Project description so future owners understand the context without asking.

A handoff without these steps is a governance gap — the new owner inherits configurations they do not understand and may not trust, leading either to misuse or to an informal rewrite that creates a second, diverging version.
hook: Handoff = read instructions, audit knowledge, verify permissions, document purpose — in that order.

front: What are the four stages of a knowledge base document's lifecycle?
back:
The four stages are: (1) **Creation** — the document is authored, reviewed, and first added to the knowledge base; (2) **Active use** — it is current and conversations draw on it regularly; (3) **Review** — a scheduled or triggered check confirms it is still accurate and in scope; (4) **Retirement** — it is removed from the knowledge base when superseded, expired, or no longer relevant, and archived off-platform if compliance requires a copy.

Skipping the retirement stage is the most common failure — documents accumulate without exit criteria, and the knowledge base fills with ghost documents that no one owns.
hook: Creation → active use → review → retirement: documents must exit, not just accumulate.

front: How do you decide whether a requirement should become an instruction or a knowledge document?
back:
Use the **imperative vs informational test**: if the requirement tells Claude *how to behave or what to do* — "always include a disclaimer", "never speculate on pricing" — it is an instruction. If the requirement provides *facts or reference content* Claude should draw on when answering — the actual disclaimer text, the pricing policy document — it is knowledge.

The boundary blurs when a knowledge document contains embedded directives ("Claude must apply Section 4 before answering pricing questions"). Those embedded directives are weaker than explicit instructions; for mandatory behaviour, always declare it in the Project instructions field.
hook: Imperative = instruction field; informational = knowledge document — embedded imperatives are weaker.

front: Name three events that should trigger a review of project instructions.
back:
First, a **change in the underlying business requirement** the instructions encoded — new tone standards, a change in what topics are in or out of scope, a policy update that changes permitted output. Second, **user feedback indicating unexpected Claude behaviour** — if Claude consistently does something the team did not intend, the instructions likely have a gap or contradiction. Third, **personnel change** — a new team member who receives different outputs than experienced users would prompt a review for clarity or implicit assumptions baked into the text.

Instructions should not be static artefacts; they require the same maintenance discipline as any procedural document.
hook: Review instructions when requirements change, behaviour surprises users, or the team composition changes.

front: How should you handle two knowledge base documents that contradict each other?
back:
Remove the incorrect or outdated one rather than adding a third document to reconcile them. **Claude has no authority to declare one document more current than another** — if both are present, it may draw on either or synthesise an inconsistent hybrid.

If both documents are still partly valid (e.g., one covers a historical policy still relevant for legacy transactions), keep them but make the scope of each unambiguous through naming and headers: "Legacy Pricing Policy (pre-2024 contracts)" vs "Current Pricing Policy (2024 onwards)". The scope qualification allows Claude to reference the right document based on context.
hook: Remove superseded content; if both are valid, add scope markers that make the boundary explicit.

front: Why does vague instruction specificity cause more harm in a shared Project than in a personal one?
back:
In a personal Project, the author of a vague instruction interprets it themselves and Claude may learn from corrections in conversation. In a **shared Project**, different team members interpret the same vague instruction differently — one treats it as permissive, another as restrictive — producing inconsistent outputs across the team.

Vagueness also makes training harder: a new team member has no basis for knowing whether their interpretation is correct. Specificity in shared instructions is a governance property, not just a quality preference. The standard for a shared Project instruction is: any team member, reading it cold, should interpret it identically.
hook: Shared Project instructions need higher specificity — multiple readers must reach the same interpretation.

front: How should you design project instructions when a team has several distinct use cases?
back:
Write instructions that capture the **common baseline** all use cases share — the shared constraints, tone, and output principles — and keep case-specific requirements in per-chat prompts or in separate sub-Projects.

Trying to encode every variant into one Project's instructions produces a sprawling, hard-to-maintain instruction set full of "if the task is X, do Y; if the task is Z, do W" branching that is fragile and difficult to audit. A cleaner design is a parent Project holding universal rules plus child Projects or prompt templates for each use case variant.
hook: Shared instructions = universal baseline only; use sub-Projects or templates for case-specific rules.

front: What quality risk increases as a knowledge base grows beyond its intended scope?
back:
**Retrieval noise** increases: a larger, less curated knowledge base means Claude retrieves more loosely related content alongside the most relevant material. Outputs may blend the truly relevant information with tangentially related content, reducing precision without the user being aware of which documents influenced the answer.

A secondary risk is the **auditing burden**: with more documents, the probability that at least one is outdated or conflicting grows, but the review effort also grows, making scheduled audits less likely to happen. Both effects compound — quality degrades while the mechanism for detecting degradation becomes harder to run.
hook: More documents = more retrieval noise and more audit burden — size is a quality risk.

front: What specific consistency problem does a shared Project solve that a shared document library cannot?
back:
A shared document library provides reference material, but it does not govern *how Claude uses* that material or *how it behaves*. Each user still writes their own prompt, which means they decide independently what to include, how to frame the task, and what constraints to impose.

A shared **Project** attaches instructions directly to the Claude interface, so behavioural constraints are applied automatically without depending on each individual to write a complete prompt. The consistency benefit is not just about content access — it is about removing the human variable in prompt quality from the output equation.
hook: Project enforces behaviour automatically; a document library just provides content anyone can ignore.

front: What is the practical difference between a Style configuration and a tone instruction in Project instructions?
back:
A **Style** is a platform-level profile that defines aesthetic properties: word choice sophistication, sentence rhythm, use of headers and lists, overall formality. It applies holistically to how Claude writes.

A **tone instruction** written into Project instructions is a behavioural directive: "Always adopt an empathetic tone when discussing claim disputes" or "Never use humour in legal memos." The instruction is contextual and specific to this Project's domain.

Styles handle the general presentation layer; instructions handle domain-specific tonal rules. Both can be active simultaneously; they serve different levels of the output specification.
hook: Style = aesthetic profile; tone instruction = domain-specific directive — both can coexist.

front: Under what conditions does a per-chat instruction override a project-level instruction?
back:
A per-chat instruction **typically overrides** a project-level instruction when it is more specific, more recent, and not explicitly flagged as non-overridable. Claude treats the conversation as the immediate context and will honour a specific request in a conversation even if the project instruction says otherwise.

However, override behaviour depends on how the project instruction is written. An instruction framed as an absolute constraint — "Under no circumstances produce output that references competitor pricing" — is more likely to be respected even under per-chat pressure than an instruction framed as a preference. The practical conclusion: framing matters, but compliance controls should not rely solely on prompt-layer instructions.
hook: Specific per-chat beats general project defaults; absolute framing resists override better than preference framing.

front: What is the precise distinction between *knowledge* and *instruction* in a Project — and why does misplacing content between them cause failures?
back:
**Knowledge** is reference material Claude retrieves and draws on: policy text, product data, guidelines. **Instructions** are directives that shape Claude's behaviour: constraints, role, format, what to include or avoid.

Misplacing content between them causes two classes of failure. Putting instructions in a knowledge document means they are *referenced* rather than *followed as rules*, so Claude may apply them inconsistently or only when the document is retrieved. Putting reference material in the instructions field bloats the behavioural directive with informational content, making the true rules harder to locate and maintain, and potentially pushing the instruction length beyond where it is reliably processed.

The architecture of a Project works correctly only when each layer holds the type of content it was designed for.
hook: Instructions govern behaviour; knowledge stores content — misplacing either degrades both reliability and maintainability.

front: How do you prevent stale knowledge from corrupting outputs in a high-velocity environment where documents change frequently?
back:
The most reliable strategy is using a **connector to the source system** rather than static uploads — the connector retrieves current content at query time, so currency is structural rather than dependent on someone remembering to update the knowledge base.

Where connectors are unavailable, mitigate with: (1) a scheduled review cadence shorter than the typical document change cycle; (2) a naming convention that includes a "valid until" or "next review" date in the filename; (3) assigning an explicit knowledge base owner who is accountable for updates.

The residual risk with any static approach is that a change in the source happens between reviews. High-velocity environments genuinely require connector-based access for documents that change faster than the review cycle.
hook: High-change data needs connectors; static uploads require a review cycle shorter than the change rate.

front: Why does instruction conflict carry higher risk in a shared Project than in a personal one?
back:
In a personal Project, the user experiences the conflict themselves, investigates it, and fixes it — the feedback loop is immediate. In a **shared Project**, different users may observe different symptoms of the same conflict and interpret them as separate problems with their own prompts, never identifying the shared root cause.

More importantly, a conflict in a shared Project may produce systematically different outputs for different team members, depending on which instruction their conversational context activates — creating invisible inconsistency that looks like normal variation rather than a configuration defect. The shared Project has no equivalent of "the author knows what they meant" to paper over ambiguity.
hook: Shared Project conflicts produce invisible, multi-person inconsistency — no single owner catches it naturally.

front: Describe a scenario where a knowledge base makes Claude *less* useful rather than more.
back:
When a knowledge base contains **contradictory, outdated, or off-scope documents**, Claude draws on that material confidently alongside correct material, blending good and bad information into outputs that are harder to verify than if no knowledge base were present at all.

A second scenario: a knowledge base loaded with **dense, poorly structured documents** degrades retrieval precision — Claude synthesises surface-level content from multiple documents rather than surfacing the precise policy or fact the user needs, producing an answer that is technically grounded but practically unhelpful.

The knowledge base adds value only when its contents are curated, current, and scoped correctly. A poorly maintained knowledge base is strictly worse than relying on Claude's general capability with a well-written per-chat prompt.
hook: Stale, conflicting, or over-stuffed knowledge base degrades outputs below baseline — curation is not optional.

front: How do project instructions relate to a system prompt, and where does the boundary lie?
back:
**Project instructions** are a product-layer abstraction that maps to what engineers call a **system prompt** — directives that precede the user's conversation and shape Claude's behaviour throughout. For most business users, they are the same thing expressed through a friendlier interface.

The distinction matters when an organisation uses both the Claude.ai product (which exposes project instructions via the UI) and the API (which allows engineers to set a system prompt directly). A developer-set system prompt may conflict with or duplicate project instructions if both layers are active. The governance question is: which layer is authoritative, and who owns it? That boundary must be agreed with the engineering team, not assumed.
hook: Project instructions are the UI expression of a system prompt — both layers must be governed together.

front: How do you design Projects for an organisation with multiple teams whose needs partially overlap?
back:
Use a **layered Project architecture**: one organisation-level Project holds the universal constraints and shared knowledge that every team must respect — compliance requirements, brand voice, legal disclaimers. Each team then has its own Project that inherits the spirit of the universal baseline but adds team-specific instructions and knowledge.

Do not attempt to encode every team's variation into a single mega-Project — the resulting instruction set becomes unmaintainable and the knowledge base fills with content only one team needs. The trade-off is some duplication of universal content across Projects vs the maintenance nightmare of centralising everything. Duplication of a stable baseline is the better choice.
hook: Universal rules in a shared baseline; team-specific needs in separate Projects — avoid one mega-Project.

front: What single property of project instructions matters most for long-term maintainability?
back:
**Single-purpose clarity**: each instruction should do exactly one thing and be unambiguous about it. An instruction that bundles multiple requirements — "Write formally, avoid legal speculation, include a disclaimer, and limit to 300 words" — is harder to update than four separate instructions, because changing one requirement forces editing the whole sentence and risks inadvertently altering the others.

Single-purpose rules are also easier to audit: you can read each rule, ask "is this still the right requirement?", and answer yes or no. Compound rules create ambiguity about *which part* is being changed.

Length, structure, and modular organisation all follow from this property — they are means to an end, not ends in themselves.
hook: One instruction, one purpose — compound rules are the root cause of most maintenance failures.
